events.credibility_reason: Known only through a one-line OEIS citation to a book page the researcher could not read; MathWorld attaches the same 2.5×10^15 figure to Sylvester's sequence, so whether it applies to Euclid numbers is unresolved.

why: The statement is a universal yes/no claim over all Euclid numbers. Vardi's 1991 result excludes square factors q² below 2.5×10^15 for every n; that is a finite check over primes q, which narrows where a counterexample could hide but settles no restriction of the question, so it is instances rather than bound (the close call; it predates the snapshot either way, and as instances cannot make the problem open_stale). Irvine's 2023 OEIS comment only restates it: none. Lord 2014 proves Euclid numbers are not perfect powers, a different property: variant. The 2025 Lean formalisation states the open problem with a sorry body: none. No AI system did any mathematics in any event.
doubts: The Vardi bound's applicability to Euclid numbers (versus Sylvester's sequence) is unverified; the book was not read. Lord 2014 was paywalled and its content is taken from Wikipedia.
